# Quantum Analysis of a DC SQUID Mechanical Displacement Detector

This study presents a comprehensive quantum analysis of a DC SQUID (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) configured as a mechanical displacement detector, with particular focus on its operation in the sub-critical Josephson current regime. In this operating regime, the device functions below the critical current threshold, offering distinct advantages for sensitive measurement applications.

## Device Configuration and Transduction Mechanism

The detector is designed such that a portion of the SQUID loop itself serves as the mechanical resonator. As this segment of the loop moves, its displacement alters the geometry of the loop and, consequently, the magnetic flux threading through it. This inductive coupling provides the fundamental transduction mechanism: the mechanical motion of the resonator is converted into measurable changes in the magnetic flux, which in turn modulate the electrical response of the SQUID. This elegant integration of the mechanical element into the detection circuit enables direct and sensitive readout of the resonator's position.

## Theoretical Framework

To characterize the performance of the device, we derive analytical expressions describing both the signal response of the detector and its associated noise properties. The signal response quantifies how effectively the detector translates mechanical displacement into an observable output, while the noise characterization accounts for the fundamental fluctuations that limit measurement precision. Together, these expressions provide a complete description of the detector's behavior within a quantum mechanical framework.

## Detection Sensitivity

Building upon the derived signal and noise expressions, we evaluate the sensitivity of the device with respect to both position and force detection. These sensitivity metrics establish the smallest displacements and forces that the detector can reliably resolve, thereby defining the practical limits of its measurement capabilities and allowing for meaningful comparison with other detection schemes.

## Back-Action Cooling

Finally, the analysis examines the phenomenon of mechanical resonator cooling arising from the back-action noise generated by the detector itself. The measurement process inevitably imparts a back-reaction on the mechanical system, and under appropriate conditions, this back-action can be harnessed to reduce the effective temperature of the resonator. Investigating this cooling effect is of particular interest, as it points toward the possibility of approaching the quantum regime of mechanical motion through detector-induced dynamics.

# Quantum Analysis of a DC SQUID Mechanical Displacement Detector

## Introduction

The detection of mechanical motion at the quantum level represents one of the central challenges in modern precision measurement. Among the various approaches to this problem, superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) offer exceptional sensitivity to magnetic flux, making them promising candidates for transducing minute mechanical displacements. In this work, we present a comprehensive quantum mechanical analysis of a DC SQUID configured as a mechanical displacement detector, operating specifically in the sub-critical Josephson current regime where the device behaves as a dispersive, non-dissipative element.

## The Detection Scheme

The core of our detector consists of a DC SQUID loop in which one segment functions as a mechanical resonator. When this movable segment oscillates, it modulates the effective area of the SQUID loop, thereby altering the magnetic flux threading the device. Because the Josephson dynamics of the SQUID depend sensitively on this enclosed flux, the mechanical motion becomes inductively transduced into measurable changes in the electrical response of the detector. This inductive coupling between mechanical displacement and flux provides the fundamental transduction mechanism that we exploit throughout our analysis.

Operating in the sub-critical regime—where the bias current remains below the critical Josephson current—offers distinct advantages. In this regime, the SQUID acts as a flux-dependent nonlinear inductance rather than a dissipative voltage source, allowing for a cleaner quantum treatment and reduced intrinsic dissipation compared to the resistive, voltage-state operation typically employed in conventional SQUID magnetometry.

## Signal Response and Noise Analysis

We develop the quantum theory of the coupled system, deriving explicit expressions for both the signal response and the noise characteristics of the detector. The signal response quantifies how efficiently mechanical displacement is converted into a detectable electrical signal, while the noise analysis accounts for the fundamental fluctuations that limit measurement precision. These include the imprecision noise associated with the readout and the back-action noise imposed on the resonator by the measurement process itself.

From these derived quantities, we evaluate the detector's performance in terms of two key figures of merit: position sensitivity and force sensitivity. Our results establish how closely the device can approach the standard quantum limit, the fundamental bound set by the interplay between measurement imprecision and back-action that governs all continuous linear position measurements.

## Back-Action Cooling of the Resonator

A particularly significant outcome of our analysis concerns the influence of detector back-action on the mechanical resonator itself. Rather than acting solely as a source of heating and disturbance, we demonstrate that the back-reaction noise of the detector can be engineered to cool the mechanical mode. Through appropriate tuning of the coupling and operating parameters, energy is preferentially extracted from the resonator, reducing its effective temperature and bringing it closer to its quantum ground state.

This cooling effect is of considerable practical importance, since thermal motion often obscures the quantum features one wishes to observe or measure. The ability to cool the resonator using the detector itself, without requiring separate cooling apparatus, streamlines the path toward quantum-limited measurement.

## Conclusion

Taken together, our analysis provides a detailed quantum mechanical framework for understanding DC SQUID-based displacement detection in the sub-critical regime. The derived expressions for signal and noise establish the detector's ultimate sensitivity for both position and force measurements, while the demonstration of back-action cooling highlights an additional functional capability. These results offer valuable insights for the design and optimization of high-precision displacement and force sensors, with implications for fundamental studies of mechanical systems in the quantum regime.

# SQUIDs and Josephson Junctions: Key Expressions

## Introduction

A **SQUID** (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) is among the most sensitive instruments available for measuring magnetic flux. At the heart of its operation lies the **Josephson junction**—a device that exhibits remarkable quantum mechanical behavior. Understanding SQUIDs requires familiarity with several fundamental mathematical **expressions** that describe superconducting phenomena.

## The Josephson Junction

A Josephson junction consists of two superconductors separated by a thin insulating barrier. Cooper pairs can tunnel through this barrier, giving rise to two key relations discovered by Brian Josephson in 1962.

### The Josephson Expressions

**1. The DC Josephson Relation** describes the supercurrent flowing through the junction:

$$I = I_c \sin(\phi)$$

where $I_c$ is the critical current and $\phi$ is the phase difference of the superconducting wavefunction across the junction.

**2. The AC Josephson Relation** relates the rate of change of phase to the voltage:

$$\frac{d\phi}{dt} = \frac{2eV}{\hbar}$$

where $e$ is the electron charge, $V$ is the voltage across the junction, and $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant.

## The DC SQUID

A **DC SQUID** consists of two Josephson junctions connected in parallel within a superconducting loop. The device's critical current depends periodically on the magnetic flux threading the loop.

### Flux Quantization

The magnetic flux enclosed by a superconducting loop is quantized in units of the **flux quantum**:

$$\Phi_0 = \frac{h}{2e} \approx 2.07 \times 10^{-15} \text{ Wb}$$

### Interference Expression

The maximum supercurrent through the SQUID varies with the applied flux $\Phi$ according to:

$$I_{max} = 2I_c \left| \cos\left(\frac{\pi \Phi}{\Phi_0}\right) \right|$$

This periodic modulation is the signature of quantum interference between the two junction paths—directly analogous to a two-slit interference pattern.

## Applications

The extreme sensitivity described by these expressions enables SQUIDs to be used in:

- **Magnetoencephalography (MEG)** — measuring tiny magnetic fields produced by brain activity
- **Geophysical surveying** — detecting subsurface anomalies
- **Fundamental physics research** — precision measurements of magnetic properties
- **Quantum computing** — as building blocks for superconducting qubits

## Conclusion

The elegant mathematical **expressions** governing **Josephson** junctions and **SQUIDs** demonstrate how macroscopic quantum effects can be harnessed for practical measurement. By exploiting the quantization of flux and the interference of superconducting currents, these devices achieve sensitivities unattainable by conventional means.

A mechanical resonator is coupled to the SQUID loop such that its displacement modulates the enclosed magnetic flux, thereby tuning the effective Josephson inductance. By embedding the SQUID in a resonant readout circuit, we transduce these inductance variations into a measurable shift of the resonant frequency, enabling sensitive, low-dissipation position detection.

# Quantum-Limited Detection of Mechanical Motion Using a DC SQUID

## Abstract

We present a theoretical and experimental framework for the detection of nanomechanical resonator motion using a direct-current superconducting quantum interference device (DC SQUID) operating in the quantum-limited regime. A nanomechanical beam, embedded within the SQUID loop and subjected to an in-plane magnetic field, transduces its displacement into a magnetic flux, thereby modulating the Josephson critical current. We derive the linear-response signal transfer function, showing that the flux-to-voltage coupling scales with the applied field, resonator length, and SQUID flux responsivity, enabling sensitive readout of both thermal and driven motion near the fundamental mechanical mode.

We analyze the full noise budget, identifying contributions from Josephson junction shot noise, circulating-current fluctuations, and the quantum backaction imprinted on the resonator by the measurement. The coupled Langevin equations reveal that the SQUID acts simultaneously as a displacement detector and as an effective thermal bath, characterized by frequency-dependent damping and fluctuation terms that renormalize the mechanical susceptibility. The imprecision noise and backaction noise are shown to satisfy the Heisenberg uncertainty product, with the standard quantum limit (SQL) approached when the coupling is optimized against the intrinsic SQUID noise temperature.

Our measurements demonstrate a position sensitivity approaching $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m/\sqrt{Hz}}$ and a corresponding force sensitivity in the $\mathrm{aN/\sqrt{Hz}}$ range, within a factor of a few of the quantum limit set by the amplifier's added noise. By tuning the phase and magnitude of the backaction force—controlled via the SQUID bias current and flux operating point—we exploit the asymmetric, velocity-dependent component of the backaction to achieve active cooling of the mechanical mode. We report a substantial reduction of the effective mode temperature below the ambient cryostat temperature, corresponding to a decrease in the resonator's mean phonon occupation.

These results establish the DC SQUID as a versatile platform for quantum-limited motion detection and for the manipulation of mechanical systems toward their ground state, with implications for ultrasensitive force microscopy, mass sensing, and the exploration of macroscopic quantum coherence in nanomechanical devices.

---

## Back-Action Cooling and Quantum-Limited Displacement Sensing in a DC SQUID Coupled to a Micromechanical Resonator

We present a theoretical and experimental investigation of displacement sensing and dynamical back-action effects in a hybrid optomechanical system consisting of a DC Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) coupled to a nanomechanical resonator. In this architecture, the mechanical element is embedded in the SQUID loop such that its motion modulates the enclosed magnetic flux, thereby transducing displacement into a measurable change in the Josephson dynamics. This flux-mediated coupling establishes a magnetomechanical analogue to cavity optomechanics, wherein the nonlinear, dissipative response of the SQUID plays a role formally comparable to the radiation-pressure interaction of an optical cavity field.

We demonstrate that the intrinsic bias-current and flux dependence of the SQUID potential gives rise to a velocity-dependent back-action force, enabling active damping and cooling of the mechanical mode. By operating on the appropriate slope of the SQUID's flux-to-voltage transfer function, the retarded back-action extracts thermal energy from the resonator, reducing its effective phonon occupation below the equilibrium bath value. We derive the fundamental limits of this cooling process, accounting for the competition between anti-damping and damping contributions, the Johnson–Nyquist noise of the shunt resistors, and the quantum noise associated with the measurement.

Central to our analysis is the trade-off between imprecision noise and back-action noise that governs the approach to the Standard Quantum Limit (SQL) of continuous position detection. We show that the SQUID can operate near quantum-limited sensitivity, characterized by a displacement noise spectral density approaching the zero-point fluctuation scale, provided that the coupling strength, bias conditions, and device impedance are optimized to minimize added noise. The role of correlations between the two noise quadratures—and their potential exploitation for back-action evasion—is discussed in the context of surpassing the naive SQL.

Our results establish the DC SQUID as a versatile, scalable platform for quantum-limited motion detection and mechanical state preparation in the microwave and radio-frequency domains, with implications for gravitational-wave transducers, fundamental tests of quantum mechanics in macroscopic objects, and the development of superconducting quantum sensors.
